message.content:
### Quick Check – Command Prompt  

Open **Command Prompt** (`cmd`) and type:

```batch
tasklist /FI "IMAGENAME eq Code.exe"
```

* What happens  
  * If Visual Studio Code is currently running, you’ll get an output similar to this:

    ```
    Image Name                     PID Session Name        Session#   Mem Usage
    ========================= ======== ================ ========= ============
    Code.exe                   12345 Console                    1     150,000 K
    ```

  * If nothing shows up under “Image Name”, you’ll see:

    ```text
    INFO: No tasks are running which match the specified criteria.
    ```

So simply look at whether there’s a row for `Code.exe`.

---

### Alternative – PowerShell

If you prefer PowerShell, you can do essentially the same thing but with more flexibility:

```powershell
Get-Process -Name Code | Format-Table Id, ProcessName, WorkingSet64
```

or even filter directly:

```powershell
if (Get-Process -Name Code -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) {
    Write-Host "VS Code is running."
}
else {
    Write-Host "VS Code is NOT running."
}
```

This will print a short confirmation instead of listing all details.

---

#### Things to Keep In Mind

| Point | Why It Matters |
|-------|----------------|
| **Case‑sensitivity** | On Windows the image name is case‑insensitive, so `"Code.exe"` works regardless of capitalization. |
| **Multiple instances** | If you’ve opened several windows, each one appears as its own `Code.exe`. All will be listed together. |
| **Admin rights** | You don’t usually need elevated permissions to query your own processes, but some system‑wide checks might require it. |

That’s all you need—just hit enter after typing the command and read the result!
